notes: Aloxe-Corton reds are fairly dark, ruby to garnet in color.
They smell and taste of red and black fruit, and they are robust and structured.
Most Alsace whites come from aromatic grapes, so many are aromatic, floral and spicy.
Riesling here is known for dry wines, and Gewürztraminer for highly aromatic ones.
Long, dry autumns let Pinot Gris hang late, often giving very powerful flavors.
Vendanges Tardives wines often show very exotic, candied fruit aromas with a fresh finish.
Anjou Blanc ranges from dry to sweet and from light to full bodied, and dry Chenin here tastes of quince and apple.
Anjou Rouge is fruity, with red fruit and a light structure, and is made to drink within three years.
Red Bandol is dark, with rich flavors of black fruit, vanilla, cinnamon and leather.
It usually needs at least 10 years to fully develop, though some is made to drink after three.
Bandol rosé is spicy and earthy, sometimes with strawberry notes.
Barsac stands out for very fruity aromas and a liveliness that comes from its limestone soils.
Most Beaujolais reds are light in color, fruity and floral, and made to drink young. Villages and cru wines are deeper and more structured, and can keep for several years.
Beaujolais Nouveau is released on the third Thursday of November. It is fresh and fruity, and meant to drink within a few months.
Producers usually use a semi-carbonic style of fermentation to keep the fruit.
Most Beaujolais is red from Gamay, usually made with a semi-carbonic style of fermentation to keep the fruit.
The northern villages make more powerful, age-worthy wines than the light, fruity reds of the south.
Beaune makes mostly red wine, lighter and more perfumed than the reds of the Côte de Nuits.
Bergerac whites and reds are dry, and its rosés are dry or off-dry.
The reds are fruity, sometimes richly tannic, and a little austere when young.
The whites are floral and fruity with some acidity, and fuller Sémillon or Muscadelle wines gain complexity over a few years.
Plain Bordeaux AOC wines are fruity, with little oak, and are made to drink young.
Left Bank reds lean on Cabernet Sauvignon and are concentrated, tannic and long lived.
Right Bank reds lean on Merlot and often have great fruit concentration and softer tannins.
Sauternes and Barsac make sweet whites from grapes affected by noble rot.
Plain Bordeaux AOC wines are fruity, with little oak, and are made to drink young.
Bourgueil reds have a floral, fruity bouquet that turns earthy as the wine ages.
Traditional red Burgundy is known for savory fleshiness and farmyard aromas, though modern styles are often lighter, cleaner and more fruit-forward.
In good years red Burgundy ages well, gaining complex fruit and forest floor flavors and often peaking 15 to 20 years after the vintage.
Well-made white Burgundy from the Côte d'Or needs at least three years in bottle to show its aromas and character.
Grand cru wines are made for cellaring and usually need at least five to seven years.
Aligoté makes light whites with slightly herbal flavor and higher acidity than Chardonnay.
It is a lightly sweet rosé, and its sweetness sets it apart from most other rosés.
Cahors is a red only, made mostly from Malbec, dark and deep in color and able to age a long time.
The wines are dark purple, with aromas of damson, tobacco and raisin.
Chablis's cool climate gives Chardonnay more acidity and less fruit than warmer regions do.
Racy, green-apple acidity is its trademark, and the style is crisper and steelier than the rest of Burgundy.
Chablis was traditionally aged in old, neutral barrels that added no oak flavor.
Some Chablis has an earthy, wet stone flavor that grows with age before mellowing into delicate honeyed notes.
Grand cru Chablis can often age well over 15 years, and many premiers crus at least 10.
Chablis's cool climate gives Chardonnay more acidity and less fruit than warmer regions do.
Racy, green-apple acidity is its trademark, and the style is crisp, lean and mineral.
Some Chablis has an earthy, wet stone flavor that grows with age before mellowing into delicate honeyed notes.
Pinot Noir gives Champagne body and structure, Chardonnay brings freshness, and Meunier adds roundness.
A dosage of sugar and wine sets the sweetness, and today it is used mostly to fine-tune the sense of acidity.
White Chassagne-Montrachet is often both fruity and mineral, with more or less oak depending on the producer.
Its vineyards are known for a hazelnut aroma, while Puligny-Montrachet is steelier.
Grenache gives very ripe, sweet juice, while Syrah adds color and spice and Mourvèdre adds elegance and structure.
The reds are often earthy and gamey, with hints of tar, leather and the dried herbs called garrigue.
White Châteauneuf ranges from lean and mineral to oily and rich, with notes such as almond, anise, fennel, honeysuckle and peach.
Chinon's Cabernet Franc reds are typically dry and light to medium bodied.
Wines from the steep, rocky slopes are more tannic, with mineral and gamey notes, and grow velvety and spicy with age.
Good producers in strong years make full bodied, well structured reds for aging.
Condrieu is made only from Viognier and is highly aromatic, with violet, white peach and apricot.
It is often full bodied and rich, with a texture like Chardonnay, and its perfume can suggest sweetness.
Too much oak can overwhelm its delicate flavors.
It is usually best within four to eight years, as its freshness fades with age.
Cornas is made only from Syrah, and its wines are almost black in color and age well.
Mercurey reds are noted for spicy cherry notes.
Montagny whites are noted for their acidity and body.
Bouzeron's Aligoté is light bodied with subtle spice, and is at its best within five years.
Reds grow lighter and more perfumed from the Côte de Nuits south through Beaune.
Meursault makes rich, buttery Chardonnay that turns nutty with time.
Corton's best reds join the muscle of the Côte de Nuits with the elegance of the Côte de Beaune.
Pommard has a solid structure with velvety fruit and long aging potential, while Volnay is prized for great finesse, its tannic frame balanced by discreet acidity.
Gevrey-Chambertin, Morey-Saint-Denis and Vougeot are noted for full bodied reds.
Chambolle-Musigny's chalky soils give lighter bodied wines with finer aromas.
Côte des Blancs Champagnes are known for light, delicate aromas, finesse and elegance.
Côte-Rôtie is known above all for its aroma, pairing meaty notes like bacon with floral ones like violet.
Common notes include green olive, raspberry, black and white pepper, blueberry, blackberry, plum and leather.
Wines from the iron-rich schist of the Côte Brune are more tannic and full bodied, and need longer in bottle.
Next to mineral, tannic Hermitage, Côte-Rôtie is fruity and perfumed.
Coteaux du Layon is a sweet Chenin Blanc white that is never dry, though the sweetness varies.
Basic wines are semi-sweet, and some producers make very sweet wines with intense botrytis character.
Next to sweet Vouvray, the wines tend to be fuller bodied, often sweeter and slightly lower in acidity.
Chenin Blanc gives them high acidity when young and the ability to age well.
The whites range from dry and citrusy to fuller and rounder.
Grenache-based Côtes du Rhône Villages typically has a chewy fruitiness.
Chenin Blanc's high acidity suits it well.
It comes in a range of sweetness levels, from dry to sweet.
Gevrey-Chambertin reds are deeply colored and potent for Burgundy.
They have intense aromas and flavors of blackcurrant, cherry, musk and licorice.
It usually benefits from at least three years in the cellar, and the best keep 10 years or more.
Its oak-aged dry Sauvignon Blanc blends are among the few Sauvignons that age well.
Sauternes and Cérons, inside Graves, make sweet whites shaped by noble rot.
Hermitage reds tend to be very earthy, with aromas of leather, red berries, earth, cocoa and coffee.
They are mineral and tannic, with a long reputation for power.
Rich, dry whites are made from Marsanne and Roussanne.
Jurançon makes a dry white and a more sought-after sweet white.
The sweet wines develop aromas of tropical fruit such as pineapple and mango.
The vins doux naturels are sweet wines fortified during fermentation to keep their sugar.
Picpoul, low in alcohol and high in acidity, is used in blends and on its own.
Red Lirac often resembles a soft Côtes du Rhône Villages, while the more ambitious wines are closer to Châteauneuf-du-Pape.
Loire wines tend to be fruity, with fresh, crisp flavors from high acidity, especially when young.
Sweetness runs from bone dry (sec) to very sweet moelleux wines, often touched by noble rot.
Sauvignon Blanc tastes of gooseberry and grapefruit, and cool years give lighter, more mineral wines.
Loire Pinot Noir is very light in body and color, and ripe Cabernet Franc smells of raspberry and pencil shavings.
Madiran, from Tannat, is typically very concentrated and high in tannin.
It traditionally needs several years of aging to be at its best.
Blackcurrant is the main fruit flavor in Margaux.
Aromas of violets are a hallmark of the appellation.
Wines from the southern communes, such as Cantenac and Labarde, tend to be more powerful, less fragrant and closer to plum.
Petit Verdot is used in small amounts here to give structure to the Bordeaux blend.
Mercurey reds are noted for spicy cherry notes, though quality varies.
The rarer whites are mineral, with apple notes.
White Meursault usually shows clear oak and malolactic fermentation, which is why it is often called buttery.
Meursault is among the roundest white Burgundies, and it turns nutty with age.
White Meursault often shows toasted almond and hazelnut notes, with butter, honey and citrus.
Monbazillac is a sweet white from Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle.
It is broadly like Sauternes, but more Muscadelle in the blend can give slightly different aromas.
Montagny whites are noted for their acidity and body.
Morgon makes earthy wines that can take on a silky, Burgundian texture after five years.
The Côte du Py hillside makes the most powerful Morgon.
It can keep developing in bottle for up to 10 years.
Moulin-à-Vent makes the fullest bodied and most powerful Beaujolais.
Some producers age it in oak, giving more tannin and structure than other Beaujolais.
It can keep developing in bottle for up to 10 years, gaining Burgundian structure and complexity.
Muscadet is made from Melon de Bourgogne and has no Muscat-like flavor.
It is light bodied, almost always dry, and has a legal maximum of 12% alcohol.
It is fresh and crisp, with citrus and mineral notes, and is best within three years of release.
Wines kept longer on their lees are slightly fuller bodied.
In cool years the grapes can lack the fruit to balance their acidity.
Northern Rhône reds are often known by their aromas of green olive and smoky bacon.
Syrah here is classically elegant, tannic and smoky, with restrained fruit.
Pauillac's main fruit flavor is usually blackcurrant, sometimes veering toward plum.
It is noted for a strong lead-pencil scent, and some wines show minty notes.
The wines are deeply colored, powerful and structured, and develop a highly complex bouquet with long aging.
Reds typically taste of blackcurrant and cedar and are often called earthy.
The whites taste of nectarine when young and of nuts, honey and custard after 7 to 15 years.
Its oak-aged Sauvignon Blanc blends are among the few Sauvignons that age well.
Pomerol is led by Merlot, with Cabernet Franc valued for the tannin and acidity it adds.
Its characteristic flavor is plum, sometimes tending to prune.
The wines are deeply colored and creamy, with supple tannins and lower acidity than other Bordeaux reds.
Clay soils give body and power, while lighter, sandier soils give less powerful wines that age less long.
The reds have soft, plump, fleshy fruit, with more of a fruitcake flavor than Pomerol.
Pommard is among the most powerful and tannic reds of the Côte de Beaune.
It contrasts with the light, elegant wines of neighboring Volnay.
Pouilly-Fuissé is a full bodied Chardonnay with aromas of nuts and yellow fruit such as lemon, pineapple and apple.
With age, honey and brioche take over.
Pouilly-Fumé is a dry Sauvignon Blanc from around Pouilly-sur-Loire.
It tastes of gooseberry and grapefruit and is usually fuller bodied and richer than other Loire Sauvignon.
It is one of the few Sauvignon Blancs with aging potential.
Provence is known mainly for rosé, which is normally dry, with zesty acidity.
Many wines carry the scents of the garrigue: wild lavender, rosemary and thyme.
Some Provence wines resemble Southern Rhône wines, sharing grapes and some of their style.
White Puligny-Montrachet is often very mineral, with more restrained oak than some other Côte de Beaune villages.
It is usually called elegant rather than fruit-driven, and it is steelier than Chassagne-Montrachet.
Young white Puligny-Montrachet is pale gold with green glints, with floral, fruity, nutty and mineral notes and a honeyed touch.
Northern Rhône reds, from Syrah, are known for aromas of green olive and smoky bacon.
Southern reds from the left bank are full bodied and tannic when young, with aromas of prune, undergrowth, chocolate and ripe black fruit.
Right bank reds are slightly lighter and fruitier.
Syrah adds structure and color to Grenache in blends such as Côtes du Rhône and Châteauneuf-du-Pape.
Reds from the left bank are full bodied and tannic when young, with aromas of prune, undergrowth, chocolate and ripe black fruit.
Right bank reds are slightly lighter and fruitier.
Rosé d'Anjou is a medium-sweet rosé made mostly from Grolleau.
Rully's better whites are crisp and lean, with lemon and nutty notes and lively acidity.
It is known as slow to mature and among the toughest, most tannic Bordeaux.
Southern Saint-Julien is smoother and close to Margaux, while the north is more robust and powerful, like Pauillac.
Its wines are noted for scents of cedar and cigar box.
Saint-Véran shows white peach, apple or pear, or floral notes of lime blossom and acacia.
With time these give way to hazelnut or almond, with touches of honey, vanilla and flint.
Classic Sancerre blanc is bone dry and highly aromatic, with intense flavors of peach and gooseberry.
It has naturally high acidity and can show flinty, gunflint notes as well as citrus and spice.
Kimmeridgian marl gives powerful Sancerre, limestone gives elegant wines, and flinty clay gives wines with white and yellow flower notes.
Red Sancerre, from Pinot Noir, is light to medium bodied and floral, and the rosés are dry with raspberry and strawberry notes.
Saumur's Cabernet Franc reds are light and fruity.
Sauternes is a sweet white from grapes touched by noble rot, and it must taste noticeably sweet.
Common notes are apricot, honey and peach, with a nutty note typical of botrytized Sémillon.
The best can age well beyond 100 years.
Savennières is a white from Chenin Blanc, today almost always dry.
Its cool climate gives it high acidity, and it is long lived.
The traditional style can be austere and closed when young.
It is fuller bodied than dry Vouvray.
It is dry, with more body and structure than most rosés.
Longer skin contact for part of the juice makes it more powerful, more tannic and darker than other rosés.
Touraine whites are dry and mainly Sauvignon Blanc, with citrus, tropical fruit or white flower aromas and a fresh finish.
Vacqueyras reds are mainly Grenache, with Syrah and Mourvèdre, and are powerful, rich and full bodied.
Volnay is typically light, aromatic and elegant rather than powerful.
Vosne-Romanée is often described as combining elegance with power.
The wines are racy and elegant, and they often need long cellaring to develop fully.
Vouvray is Chenin Blanc, made from dry (sec) through off-dry (demi-sec) to sweet (moelleux and doux), and sparkling.
Cool years favor dry and sparkling wines, while warm years bring sweet and even botrytized wines.
Depending on style, it shows honey, nuts, ginger, fig, apple and white flowers.
Traditional high-acid examples can need three to seven years in bottle before the acidity softens.
Côtes de Gascogne wines show aromatic freshness, mostly fruity or floral.
Their intensity varies with the grape and how the wine is made.
Wines with some sweetness, and the late-harvest whites, have riper, more developed fruit aromas.
Madiran, from Tannat, is typically very concentrated and high in tannin.
Jurançon is a sweet white from Gros and Petit Manseng, and Jurançon Sec is its dry version.
